metadata.title: Statue of Sobek
metadata.description: This is a fragment of a limestone statue (snout restored) of the chief god of the Fayum, the crocodile-headed Sobek. The statue comes from the mortuary temple of Amenemhat III, attached to his pyramid at Hawara. Known as 'The Labyrinth' in classical times, the temple was described by Herodotus as surpassing even the pyramids as a marvel

English:
The presentation explores the history of the discovery of radioactivity, the fundamentals of radiobiology, and the effects of ionizing radiation on the human body. It examines Ukraine's nuclear infrastructure, the consequences of the Chornobyl disaster, and contemporary risks associated with the Zaporizhzhia Nuclear Power Plant, nuclear threats, and radiation safety. Particular attention is given to practical recommendations for public safety and appropriate actions in the event of a radiation emergency.

metadata.title: 'Electron tunneling' inside a respiratory enzyme: the secret of a low reorganization energy
metadata.description:
• Using two independent calculations — molecular dynamics and quantum chemistry — the researchers showed that the electron transfer between the two hemes (heme a and heme a₃) in cytochrome c oxidase (CcO, Complex IV), the last enzyme of the respiratory chain, occurs with an exceptionally low reorganization energy (about 0.2 eV, roughly a third of the usual 0.7 eV)
  • The key to this low reorganization energy was the water molecules packed around the hemes; in the calculations, switching off the interactions with water made the reorganization energy surge to about 0.5 eV
  • To reproduce the experimentally measured nanosecond-scale electron transfer rate even under a low reorganization energy, the researchers introduced a method that averages over every atom pair between donor and acceptor rather than using a single shortest distance between the two hemes; this suggests there is no need to assume any specific single tunneling pathway. That said, this is a computational study, and the experimental value of the reorganization energy itself remains under debate


[Quantum Biology Society]

Where does the oxygen we breathe in ultimately go inside the body? Its final destination is cytochrome c oxidase (CcO), which sits at the very end of the respiratory chain in the mitochondria of our cells. This enzyme, also known as Complex IV, binds four electrons and four protons to a single molecule of dioxygen (O₂) and reduces it to two molecules of water. The ultimate reason we breathe lies precisely in this chemical reaction. With the energy released in the process, the enzyme pumps protons across the cell membrane, and the proton concentration gradient thus formed goes on to synthesize ATP, the energy currency of life.


But inside this enzyme the electron must leap across a considerable distance. The di-copper centre (CuA) that first receives the electron, for instance, sits about 20 Å — centre to centre — from its next stop, heme a. How can an electron jump such a distance through a protein, an excellent insulator? The answer lies in quantum mechanics. The electron moves by quantum tunneling, passing straight through an enormous energy barrier. And exactly what controls the speed of that leap is the central question of this study.


A study published in the Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences (PNAS) in 2010 (vol. 107, no. 50) used careful computer calculations to probe the factors that set the rate of this tunneling. A team from the University of Helsinki in Finland (Ville Kaila, Mikael Johansson and colleagues), together with the group of Mårten Wikström, an authority in bioenergetics, analysed the electron transfer between the two hemes using two independent methodologies: molecular dynamics (MD) simulation and quantum chemical calculation. They found that this electron transfer, unlike the majority of biological reactions, has an exceptionally low reorganization energy — and yet demonstrated that its rate can be well described by the classic predictive formula for biological electron transfer, the Moser–Dutton equation.


■ The final destination of a breath: the enzyme that turns oxygen into water

CcO serves as the final electron drain of catabolic metabolism. It accepts electrons and protons to reduce oxygen to water, and, intriguingly, the two particles enter from opposite sides of the membrane. The electrons come from the soluble carrier cytochrome c on the positive (P) side, and the protons from the negative (N) side. This movement of charge alone establishes an electrochemical proton gradient across the membrane.


On top of this, CcO pumps an additional proton across the membrane for every electron it carries. This doubles the energy efficiency compared with the classical Mitchellian scheme. In short, the enzyme is a redox-driven proton pump that harnesses the energy generated in turning oxygen into water to pump protons.


The electron's route runs step by step from cytochrome c to the copper centre CuA, then to the low-spin heme a, and on to heme a₃ and the copper centre CuB — the binuclear site where oxygen is reduced. Of these, the electron's hop from heme a to heme a₃ (the binuclear site) is the main stage of this study, and it is intricately coupled to the movement of a proton.


■ The electron crosses by tunnel: distance and reorganization energy

Here it is worth noting a fundamental difference in the physical properties of electron and proton. The proton is about 2,000 times heavier than the electron. The light electron, following the laws of quantum mechanics, can cross even long distances easily by tunneling, whereas the heavy proton is severely restricted in leaping and generally moves by shifting along a hydrogen-bonded network — the Grotthuss mechanism. It is precisely this tunneling that lets the electron cross the 20 Å gap between CuA and heme a.


The rate of this tunneling is described by the semiclassical Marcus theory. Three key variables govern the electron transfer rate: the electronic coupling between donor and acceptor, the driving force of the reaction (ΔG), and the reorganization energy (λ). Of these, the reorganization energy is the protagonist of this study.

The reorganization energy is the energy consumed as the surrounding atoms and water molecules rearrange to match the new charge distribution when the electron moves from donor to acceptor. When this value is large, electron transfer slows down — as though every piece of furniture had to be rearranged in a new house — while when it is small, little changes in the environment and the electron can move quickly and smoothly. In ordinary biological electron transfer, this value has been taken to be roughly 0.7 eV.


■ A surprisingly low reorganization energy, and its secret was water

The reorganization energy of CcO, calculated by two independent methods, came in at less than half the usual value. Molecular dynamics gave about 0.2 eV for both the forward and backward directions, and high-level quantum chemical calculation gave about 0.13 eV. Two different methodologies arrived at strikingly similar figures.

To find the cause of such a low value, the researchers controlled the surrounding environment in the simulation one element at a time. When the protein environment around the hemes was frozen into a fully oxidized structure, the reorganization energy rose to about 0.33 eV. Crucially, when the interactions with water molecules were then also switched off, the value shot up further to about 0.52 eV. The water packed densely around the hemes was the key to producing the low reorganization energy.


Water molecules behave like tiny compasses (dipoles) that nimbly change orientation according to charge. Each time heme a is reduced and its charge changes, the water molecules flexibly swing around to embrace the new charge in a stable way. This supple rearrangement raises the environment's responsiveness and dramatically lowers the reorganization energy.

The fact that the two hemes sit so close together — a mere 7 Å or so at their edges — also plays a part. When the distance is short, the two hemes come to share the same cushion of surrounding environment, so that when the donor side is reduced, the environment around the acceptor is already tidied up in advance, and there is little further rearrangement to do once the electron actually arrives. It is like two people under a single blanket: when one changes position, the other's side gets roughly straightened out too.


So why do the two hemes sit so close? Because of the proton pump. The pump's key reaction is the reduction of heme a, which raises the acidity of the proton-loading site (PLS) and makes it grip a proton firmly. This loading site must therefore be close to heme a — and since the release of the loaded proton is driven by proton uptake into the binuclear site (heme a₃), it must be close to heme a₃ as well. In the end, the evolutionary function of the proton pump has placed the two hemes right up against each other, and this physical proximity results in the low reorganization energy and fast electron transfer.


■ Recalibrating the Moser–Dutton ruler: no specific pathway needed

A widely known empirical formula for predicting biological electron transfer rates is the Moser–Dutton equation. Treating the protein as a uniform medium with an average packing density, it has done an excellent job of matching rates from the donor–acceptor distance and driving force alone.


Here an intriguing paradox arises. Plug the usual reorganization energy of 0.7 eV and the 7 Å distance between the two hemes into this formula, and it matches the experimentally measured rate (a time constant of about 1.4 nanoseconds) almost perfectly. But put in the actual reorganization energy this study uncovered, 0.2 eV, and the formula predicts a rate of about 40 picoseconds — more than twenty times faster. In other words, the overly high conventional value had been coincidentally cancelling out another error to land on the right answer.


To fix this, the researchers overhauled the way distance is handled. Instead of using only the single shortest edge-to-edge distance between the two hemes, they computed the distance and packing density separately for every atom pair making up the donor and acceptor, and then averaged them. This reflects the physical reality that when an electron enters or leaves a heme, the charge change is distributed across the entire heme ring rather than at a single point. Calculated this way, a rate consistent with the experimental result emerged even under the improbably low reorganization energy of 0.2 eV.


This result suggests that when the electron moves between the hemes, it need not be confined to any specific single tunneling pathway, like a thin wire; rather, tunneling occurs broadly across the entire facing surface of the two hemes. It is a fresh perspective, in direct contrast to the prevailing view that CcO makes use of a specific tunneling pathway.


■ Significance and limits

The overall catalytic turnover rate of CcO is slow, on the order of once per millisecond, and even its fastest step — oxygen binding — is on the microsecond scale. So why would a tunneling rate as blisteringly fast as the nanosecond range be needed at all?


The researchers offer two functional hypotheses. First, the electron's rapid arrival enables a kinetic trapping that holds the bound oxygen firmly at the binuclear site, dramatically raising the apparent affinity. Second, the swift electron transfer from heme a to the binuclear site pins the proton to be pumped firmly at the loading site, cutting off the back-leakage by which it might otherwise slip in reverse. In sum, driving electron transfer to the extreme is an indispensable safeguard for minimizing energy loss in this exquisite molecular machine.


There are, however, points to keep in mind when interpreting this paper. That the reorganization energy is low is a conclusion reached in common by two independent simulations (molecular dynamics and quantum chemistry) — but theoretical prediction of biological reorganization energies is itself a notoriously difficult area, and debate over the experimental value itself is still ongoing. Likewise, the conclusion that no specific tunneling pathway is needed should be seen as part of a methodological debate over how to model short-distance electron transfer.


Even so, the microscopic scene this study paints of life is a marvel. In the very instant that the oxygen we breathe in at every moment is reduced to the water of life, the electron pours through the entire facing surface of the two hemes — made possible by the supple dance of the water molecules surrounding the hemes and the meticulous structural design of the protein that binds the two hemes close together.

metadata.description: FIGURE 2. Description of Lacerta teguixin in Seba (1734: p. 150–151). Latin and French texts are not equal and can be translated as: LATIN SECTION No. 1. Tecuixin lizard, smaller, or Teiuguacu, from New Spain. The scales of the skin are deeply imbued with a saturated cerulean hue, variegated above with the palest bluish-white and white, especially upon the head, thighs, and feet. The tail, even unto its extremity, is wholly adorned with ribbon-like bands. No. 2. Another Tecuixin lizard, or Teiuguacu. In color this one indeed agrees with the former smaller one, yet in its marvelous ornamentation and variegation, here wrought by Nature, it surpassed the other. Let the mind, astonished, marvel at this inimitable ornament, and among created things so varied in color and disposition, behold and adore the omnipotent Creator. FRENCH SECTION No. 1. Small lizard named Tecuixin, or Teiuguacu, from New Spain. The scales which cover its skin are of a turquoise blue, mingled with white and an extremely pale blue, principally upon the head, thighs, and feet. Its tail is entirely adorned with bands fashioned like ribbons. No. 2. Another Tecuixin or Teiuguacu lizard, larger. Its color is the same as that of the preceding one, yet it surpasses it in the admirable variety of markings with which Nature has embellished it. One cannot contemplate this inimitable ornament, so varied among different animals, without being struck with astonishment, and without rising unto a profound adoration of the First Cause of all things.

metadata.title: El discurso femenino en la escritura de la colombiana Marvel Luz Moreno Abello
metadata.description: Marvel Luz Moreno Abello, nacida en Barranquilla (Colombia) en 1939, fue autodidacta en literatura y ciencias humanas. A partir de los años 70 se hace partícipe de la vida cultural parisina, convirtiéndose París en su segundo hogar. Su escritura da testimonio de que la cultura latinoamericana es, por tradición, falocrática y paternalista por lo que tiene la necesidad de proyectar un discurso femenino que critica a la cultura patriarcal, a la vez que se cuentan con enfoques feministas, de la sexualidad, la tradición modernista, de frontera, la vida cotidiana, la sociedad y la ciudad, relaciones entre región, nación y cosmopolitismo, entre otros.

metadata.title: Entre a Legalidade e a Consciência a Escolha Institucional de Steve Rogers em Tempos de Crise
metadata.description: O presente trabalho tem como objetivo analisar, sob a perspectiva do Direito Constitucional, o conflito entre legalidade e liberdade individual, a partir da conduta do personagem Capitão América na saga Civil War (2006–2007), publicada pela Marvel Comics. A pesquisa justifica-se pela relevância do debate acerca dos limites do poder estatal e da proteção dos direitos fundamentais em contextos de crise. Adotou-se metodologia qualitativa, de natureza teórico-bibliográfica, com base em estudo de caso narrativo. A análise é fundamentada em teorias da desobediência civil, especialmente nas contribuições de Ronald Dworkin e John Rawls,bem como na pesquisa sobre o direito de resistência. Os resultados indicam que a desobediência civil pode ser compreendida como instrumento legítimo de defesa dos direitos fundamentais, especialmente quando há violação por parte do Estado. Conclui-se que a narrativa analisada ultrapassa o campo da ficção, permitindo reflexões relevantes sobre a tensão entre legalidade e legitimidade no Estado Democrático de Direito.

metadata.title: Revealing the Mystery of Emotions in  Sounds  The Theory of Musical Equilibration Explains the Impact of  Ordered Sounds as the Listener's Identification with  Processes of Will
metadata.description:
Science has long been concerned with the question of how it is possible for music to elicit 
emotions‒so far, however, with only moderate success. The theory of musical 
equilibration shines a light on this problem from a new perspective. The theory was first 
proposed in 1997 by German music theorist, Bernd Willimek, who further developed it 
with his wife and fellow theorist, Daniela Willimek. Music itself, the theory goes, cannot 
generate emotions directly. Rather, emotions should be understood as a response to the 
processes of will that are encoded in music. By identifying with these processes of will, 
listeners experience music emotionally. This is comparable to the situation of moviegoers 
who identify with the protagonist on screen and thereby vicariously experience 
emotions. In this work, the affirmative character of the major triad and the negative 
character of the minor triad are substantiated. According to the theory of musical 
equilibration, the volume at which a minor chord is played determines whether it is 
perceived as sorrow or anger. Furthermore, the authors discuss issues such as why a 
diminished seventh chord is well-suited as the score for film scenes involving fear, or how 
an augmented chord can convey amazement and astonishment. To show the practical 
application of the theory of musical equilibration, the authors carried out tests with 
school (K-12) and university students (basic test part A, basic test part B, Rocky test).
